extracted.intended_audience: general readers, TV viewers, producers, and researchers interested in America's Got Talent format and production
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the procedural rules, format changes, selection mechanisms, and production requirements described for America's Got Talent and its spin-offs across seasons. Useful for understanding how acts advance, what special rounds exist, and how production adapts (e.g., safety or pandemic measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Golden Buzzer (general function)
rubrics_metrics.description: A special buzzer mechanism introduced into the show's format (originating on Germany's Got Talent and Britain’s Got Talent) used to save/send an act forward during auditions and later to send a participant directly into the live rounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usage has varied by season: initially used mainly to save an act from elimination in auditions; later standardized across the Got Talent franchise to send an act directly into live rounds. Restrictions have applied in some seasons (e.g., host not allowed to use it in certain seasons). Examples: Season 9 introduced Golden Buzzer (used mainly to save an act); from Season 10 forward its use would send participants directly into live rounds. Season 11 allowed the host to use it during auditions; Season 19 changed allotments (see related entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Golden Buzzer (seasonal allotments and restrictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Season-specific rules about who can use the Golden Buzzer and how many times it may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the page: in some seasons the host was not allowed to use it; Season 11 allowed the host (Nick Cannon) to use it during auditions; Season 19 increased audition Golden Buzzers so each judge received two Golden Buzzers (up from one) and, for the first time on the American version, each judge was allowed one Golden Buzzer during the live shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boot Camp → Judge Cuts format and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The intermediate post-audition elimination round (originally called 'boot camp') was revamped and renamed 'Judge Cuts' with a new multi-week structure and guest-judge involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Cuts consisted of about eighty acts shortlisted from the auditions, held over four weeks with around twenty per week, and featured a guest judge each episode. Guest judges, along with main judges, could use the Golden Buzzer to send an act to the live rounds. Later seasons reduced the number of participants (e.g., season 13 reduced to seventy-two with ~18 performing each week). During the COVID-19-affected season the Judges Cuts were drastically changed, effectively condensed into a single episode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online/Viewer Save (Snapple Vote / Dunkin' Save / Dunkin' Save expansion)
rubrics_metrics.description: An online viewer-vote mechanism (named for sponsors) used to determine which mid-range acts advance from certain rounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally 'Snapple Vote', renamed 'Dunkin' Save' for a sponsor change. Its format determined which three acts placed in the mid-range of the public vote (e.g., 5th, 6th and 7th in the semi-finals; 4th, 5th and 6th in the 'Top 12' round) would advance, with remaining acts chosen by judges. The format later expanded to cover quarter-finalists finishing 6th–8th and semi-finalists finishing 4th–6th per public vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage auditions: producer auditions and judge auditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Audition process starts with producer auditions across many cities, followed by judge auditions filmed for broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producer auditions take place in numerous cities (examples across seasons include Tampa, Nashville, Richmond, New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, etc.). Judge auditions are filmed later (often at a central venue such as the Pasadena Civic Auditorium) and are the ones aired. During the COVID-19 era, auditions were opened to virtual or recorded-video submissions for judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special 'extreme' auditions / safety handling of dangerous acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A dedicated audition session for acts considered too dangerous for indoor studio sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a special 'extreme' audition session held in Pomona, California on an outdoor stage, for participants with acts considered too dangerous to be conducted within an indoor studio set. This indicates a production safety requirement to move high-risk performances to appropriate venues and setups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest judge involvement and responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Guest judges are used in Judge Cuts (and sometimes live rounds), and may have the authority to advance acts including via the Golden Buzzer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each Judge Cuts episode featured a guest judge who, along with the main judges, could use the Golden Buzzer. Examples of guest judges across seasons: Neil Patrick Harris, Michael Bublé, Marlon Wayans, Piers Morgan, Ne-Yo, Reba McEntire, George Lopez, Louis Tomlinson, Chris Hardwick, DJ Khaled, Laverne Cox, Seal, Ken Jeong, Olivia Munn, Martina McBride, Brad Paisley, Dwyane Wade, Ellie Kemper, Jay Leno, etc. Guest judges have been used to decide advancement and to add star power to the selection stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live-round production and location changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and practices around where live rounds are filmed and how production responds to personnel or situational changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Stern's departure led to live-round broadcasts moving back to Los Angeles and being filmed at the Dolby Theatre. During COVID-19, live rounds were filmed at Universal Studios Hollywood with a virtual audience. Live-round location choices may be influenced by judge availability and production logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pandemic-related production adaptations
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational and format changes implemented to minimize COVID-19 infection risk among participants, judges, and crew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures included suspending production when sickness occurred, discontinuing live audiences, using a virtual audience, condensing or altering rounds (Judge Cuts condensed to a single episode), expanding the number of quarter-finalists, filming at alternate locations, and using guest judges to cover for absences (e.g., after Simon Cowell's injury).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for spin-offs (The Champions / All-Stars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles governing which acts are eligible for all-star/spin-off competitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Champions and All-Stars series feature winners, finalists, fan favorites, and other notable acts from previous seasons of AGT and the wider Got Talent franchise. The spin-offs are pre-recorded when held and later broadcast; The Champions was conceived as a global competition consisting of participants that had appeared across the Got Talent franchise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spin-off thematic/genre focus (e.g., AGT: Extreme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin-offs may be focused on a specific subject-matter or act-type, with production and venue tailored accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: AGT: Extreme focuses on daredevil acts; filming occurred at Atlanta Motor Speedway and production considered specific staging and safety. Cowell serves as an executive producer and judge for the series - spin-off formats may require different production resources and judges with appropriate expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format experiments and seasonal rule changes (participant counts, rounds, and scheduling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Season-to-season changes affecting number of participants in rounds, scheduling, and episode structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Judge Cuts originally ~80 acts over four weeks (~20/week), later reduced to 72 (~18/week). Seasons typically air May–September, with networks keeping runs limited to before the next TV season; scheduling can vary in Olympic years. The number of quarter-finalists was expanded in the pandemic season. Such experiments alter how many acts advance and the cadence of the broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live-show ancillary products: tours and residencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-show live touring/residency arrangements for top finalists are part of the franchise operation and selection considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: America's Got Talent Live was a post-show run in Las Vegas featuring top finalists, later remade into a 25-city tour and then into a series of shows and residencies (e.g., Planet Hollywood Resort in Las Vegas). Selection for tours/residencies has included winners and popular finalists (examples listed by season).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast ratings and scheduling considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Program scheduling and episode types affect ratings; network scheduling decisions respond to ratings patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audition and performance shows rate higher than results shows; finales often rate lower due to competing programming. The show has historically averaged ~12 million viewers but varies by season. These audience/ratings patterns influence how the network schedules the show (May–September run, adjustments in Olympic years) and may inform format decisions to maximize viewership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge and host contract/availability impacts on format
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in judge/host personnel (departures, hiring, injuries) can force format, location, or scheduling changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Howard Stern's departure led to live rounds moving to Los Angeles; Simon Cowell replacing Stern affected judge lineup; Simon Cowell's on-set injury resulted in guest judges appearing and altered production decisions. Judge/host availability may determine who can use special privileges (e.g., host Golden Buzzer) or require guest judges to fill roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contestant submission modalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepted methods for contestants to submit auditions vary and can include in-person producer auditions, virtual/recorded video submissions, and special online virtual auditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically producer auditions across cities were primary; in pandemic-affected seasons, participants were asked to provide auditions virtually or via recorded video for judgment. The show has also run virtual audition events (e.g., MySpace virtual audition referenced earlier). Submission modality affects how acts are screened and shortlisted.
